Trying to Conceive

Can particular foods help you conceive twins?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

It is natural to wonder whether food can influence the chance of twins. Here is how to separate useful preconception nutrition from claims that a particular ingredient can choose the number of babies.

Can a meal plan increase the chance of twins?

The idea of welcoming two babies together can feel exciting. It also makes lists of foods that promise twins especially appealing. The difficulty is that a food can be nutritious without changing how many eggs are released or whether an embryo divides. No particular food or everyday dietary combination has been established as a reliable way to conceive twins.

Research into diet and fertility is not the same as research into deliberately producing a twin pregnancy. Studies may compare groups with different eating habits, but those groups can also differ in age, ancestry, health, family history and use of fertility treatment. An association cannot tell an individual what to eat to obtain a particular outcome.

How twins develop and what affects the chance

Identical, or monozygotic, twins begin when one fertilised egg divides into two embryos. Non-identical, or dizygotic, twins develop when two separate eggs are fertilised. The often-quoted chance of about 1 in 250 concerns identical twins; it is not the overall natural twinning rate for every population.

A tendency to release more than one egg can run in the family of the person who ovulates. Non-identical twinning also varies with age and population background. Height and body size have been associated with twinning in observational research, but associations are not instructions to gain weight or delay pregnancy. Neither step is a sensible way to pursue twins.

Ovulation-stimulating medicines can cause several eggs to develop. IVF can result in multiples, particularly when more than one embryo is transferred. IUI places sperm in the uterus; its multiple-pregnancy risk depends especially on whether stimulation is used and how many follicles develop. These procedures have different mechanisms and should not be grouped as equivalent methods of choosing twins.

Fruit and vegetables support nutrition, not a twin guarantee

Apples, mangoes, bananas, watermelon and kiwi can all be ordinary parts of a varied diet. Carrots, broccoli and Brussels sprouts offer further variety. These foods supply different combinations of fibre and micronutrients; the benefit comes from meeting nutritional needs, not from a proven ability to trigger two eggs.

There is no validated fruit-and-vegetable schedule for twin conception, and eating larger quantities does not establish a larger effect. Choose foods you enjoy and can obtain regularly. A frozen vegetable, a familiar piece of fruit or a seasonal option can be a practical choice without turning meals into a fertility experiment.

Sunflower seeds are a food, not an ovulation treatment

Sunflower seeds can add texture and variety to meals or snacks. Claims that their vitamin content increases the likelihood of twins go beyond the evidence. Testimonials from people who ate them and later had twins cannot show that the seeds caused the pregnancy outcome.

The specific suggestion that vitamin B6 in sunflower seeds is a twin-producing treatment is unproven. There is also no reason to take extra B6 or large quantities of seeds for this purpose. If you like them, use them as one food among many and choose an alternative if you have an allergy.

Folate matters for development, not choosing the number of babies

Leafy vegetables, asparagus, avocado, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and beans can contribute folate. Before conception, folic acid supplementation has an established role in reducing neural tube defects, including spina bifida. That is the reason to take it; increasing the chance of twins is not an accepted indication.

NHS guidance recommends 400 micrograms daily while trying to conceive and through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. Some people need a prescribed higher dose because of particular medical or pregnancy risks. Follow the advice applicable to you rather than taking extra tablets to pursue twins.

Although liver contains folate, it is not a suitable fertility food to add indiscriminately. During pregnancy, liver and liver products should be avoided because of their high preformed vitamin A content. Check supplements for retinol too. Folate-rich food does not replace the recommended folic acid supplement.

Okra leaves do not have a demonstrated twin-producing effect

Okra and its leaves appear in traditional accounts of communities with frequent twin births. Their use in cooking and their nutritional content do not establish a treatment effect. A claim that a plant supplies fibre, iron or vitamin C is a different claim from saying it makes double ovulation more likely.

If okra is part of your normal food culture, you do not need to avoid it because of this discussion. Equally, you do not need to seek out unfamiliar leaves, extracts or concentrated preparations to improve your chances. Preparation and food safety still matter, and an extract should not be assumed equivalent to a cooked food.

Meat is not a requirement for conceiving twins

Meat can supply protein and other nutrients, but the suggestion that vegetarians must start eating it to have twins is not supported by a reliable treatment trial. A lower or higher twin rate in one dietary group does not tell us what would happen if one person changed their diet.

A vegetarian or vegan eating pattern should be planned to meet preconception needs, including attention to nutrients that may need supplementation. That is a question of nutritional adequacy, not a reason to abandon personal food choices in pursuit of twins. A dietitian can help if your diet is restricted or you have difficulty meeting your needs.

What the dairy study actually showed

A 2006 paper by Gary Steinman reported a twinning rate among vegan women that was one-fifth of the rate among vegetarian and omnivorous women. It proposed a connection involving insulin-like growth factor, or IGF. This is the origin of many claims that dairy increases the chance of twins fivefold.

The finding did not come from assigning people a dairy treatment and demonstrating that it produced twins. It cannot establish a dose, prove that milk caused the difference, or predict your personal chance. It also does not show that adding milk hormones directly triggers double ovulation.

Choose dairy or suitable alternatives for nutrition, tolerance and preference. Do not increase dairy beyond your needs, tolerate allergic symptoms or stop a well-planned plant-based diet because of this single association. A striking relative figure is not a personalised fertility recommendation.

Zinc supports normal function without selecting twins

Shellfish, whole grains and legumes are among the foods associated with zinc intake. Zinc is relevant to normal reproductive health, but improving an inadequate nutrient intake and causing a twin pregnancy are separate questions. Sperm count or movement alone does not determine whether two eggs are released or an embryo splits.

Do not take high-dose zinc as a twin-conception supplement. If a clinician identifies a deficiency or another reason for supplementation, use the recommended amount. Preparing foods safely also remains important when pregnancy is possible; the claimed fertility benefit does not override ordinary food-safety advice.

Whole grains and legumes are useful without a special fertility label

A meal pattern containing whole grains, beans, lentils, chickpeas, vegetables and sweet potatoes can provide fibre and a range of nutrients. Calling these complex carbohydrates does not mean they stimulate the ovaries to release extra eggs. Nor does one food pattern guarantee prevention of birth defects.

The useful aim is a varied, sustainable diet that meets your needs. Avoid turning a list of supposedly powerful carbohydrates into an obligation to eat excessive portions or to exclude other food groups. If diabetes, digestive symptoms or another condition affects your choices, obtain individual advice.

Pineapple core and bromelain are not proven implantation aids

Pineapple contains bromelain, a group of enzymes that is also sold in concentrated supplements. Claims about inflammation, uterine blood flow and implantation are often extended into promises about twins. Those steps have not been established as a reliable chain of effects in people trying to conceive.

Eating pineapple as a food does not guarantee conception, implantation or twins. A bromelain supplement is a different exposure from a serving of fruit, and its safety during pregnancy is not well established. Check with your clinician before using concentrated products, especially alongside medicines or fertility treatment.

Yams, potatoes and reports from high-twinning communities

Stories about Igbo-Ora in Nigeria often link its frequent twin births to local foods, including yams and okra leaves. Such observations are interesting starting points for research, but they cannot separate diet from inherited tendencies and other population factors. They do not establish a reproducible food prescription.

Yams, ordinary potatoes and sweet potatoes are different plants and should not be treated as interchangeable hormonal treatments. The suggestion that a plant compound acts like an ovulation medicine in the human body requires direct evidence. Neither eating more potatoes nor using a wild-yam product is a proven way to choose twins.

Plan for a healthy pregnancy and get advice when needed

A preconception appointment can address your medicines, supplements, nutrition and any fertility concerns. Bring the actual labels of products you are considering. This gives your clinician something specific to check instead of relying on claims such as natural, fertility boosting or hormone balancing.

Twin pregnancies can be healthy, but they require additional care and have higher risks, including premature birth and some maternal complications. Fertility treatment therefore aims to achieve a healthy pregnancy while reducing avoidable multiple-pregnancy risk. Do not obtain or adjust ovulation medicines simply to pursue twins.

If twins are confirmed, follow the scan and monitoring plan recommended for their placental arrangement. Before that point, you can support your health without making yourself responsible for selecting the number of babies. A singleton pregnancy does not mean that you ate the wrong foods.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Specific foods have not been established as a reliable treatment for conceiving twins.

Observational diet findings cannot be converted into a personal dose or guarantee.

How BeMama can help

Use a varied diet and an individual preconception plan; bring supplements and fertility claims to your clinician.

When to seek help

Do not use extra supplements or ovulation medicines to pursue twins. Twin pregnancies need an individual monitoring plan.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Identical and non-identical twins develop differently.
  • The one-in-250 estimate refers to identical twins.
  • All ten food claims need to be separated from ordinary nutritional benefits.
  • Take folic acid for neural tube defect prevention, not twinning.
  • Fertility treatment seeks a healthy pregnancy with avoidable risks reduced.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a proven food that makes twins more likely?

No food has been established as a reliable twin-conception treatment. A nutritious ingredient can support health without affecting the number of eggs released or embryos formed.

Does the one-in-250 figure describe all twins?

No. That estimate concerns identical twins. Non-identical twinning varies with population, inherited ovulation tendencies, age and fertility treatment, so it should not be used as one universal overall rate.

Should I drink more milk because of the fivefold claim?

The claim comes from a 2006 comparison of dietary groups, not a trial showing that adding milk causes twins. It provides no validated milk dose and no personalised prediction.

Can a vegetarian or vegan conceive twins?

Yes. Dietary labels do not rule out twins. Focus on meeting preconception nutritional needs rather than changing your ethical or personal food choices to follow an unproven twin-producing diet.

Should I take extra folic acid for twins?

No. Use the dose recommended for neural tube defect prevention and your own risk factors. A higher prescribed dose can be appropriate for specific reasons, but wanting twins is not one of them.

Are liver and folate-rich vegetables interchangeable?

No. Liver contains high levels of preformed vitamin A and should be avoided during pregnancy. Vegetables can contribute folate, while the recommended folic acid supplement still has a separate role.

Do pineapple core or bromelain improve the chance of twins?

There is no reliable evidence establishing that effect. Concentrated bromelain supplements are different from eating fruit, and pregnancy safety is not well established.

Do yams and okra explain why some communities have more twins?

Food traditions alone cannot establish the cause of a population difference. Genetics and other factors may also contribute; the observation does not provide a proven diet for someone elsewhere.

Does IUI itself make two eggs develop?

IUI places sperm inside the uterus. The risk of multiples depends especially on any accompanying ovulation stimulation and the number of follicles, rather than the insemination step alone.

Why do fertility clinics try to reduce multiple pregnancies?

Twins bring additional maternal and infant risks and require more monitoring. Clinics balance the chance of pregnancy with safety, rather than using treatment to promise a preferred number of babies.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
